intro: Before you rises the Theatre of Aspendos, from AD 155 — the most completely preserved theatre of antiquity. Its seating bank and stage building are bonded into a single block. So why did it come down to us intact? Because the Seljuqs kept it in use, as a caravanserai.
spot-1: Now you are looking at the orchestra. This is where the chorus and the musicians stood, a space 23.9 metres across.
spot-2: Now you are looking at the scaenae frons. Two storeys of aediculae and five doorways: this wall was the scenery itself, the backdrop to every performance.
spot-3: Now you are looking at the diazoma, the walkway that splits the seating in two. From here the crowd spread out to their rows.
spot-4: Now you are looking at the cavea. Forty rows of seats, cut into wedges by ten stairways. Imagine every one of them full.
spot-5: Now you are looking at the upper gallery, the vaulted gallery over the arcade. It gave the top row both its shade and its entrance.
spot-6: Now you are looking at the velarium masts. Count the post holes: there are fifty-eight. They carried the awning that kept the sun off the audience.
uncertainty: Finally, an honest word about what this model does not know. The row count is derived, not measured: the slope between the 96 m outer diameter and the 23.9 m orchestra is divided into 40 rows at a tread of 0.75 m, allowing for the vaulted gallery on top. The arrangement of the stage wall — its two storeys of aediculae, its five doorways, the rows of square sockets left by its beams — is read off photographs of the building. The statuary of that front, its wooden roof and the awning are not modelled. And the sloping wooden sounding-board over the stage was already lost in antiquity.
